# Amazon S3: say it

<!-- speak:start id=s3-s01 -->
### Prompt 1

**A customer asks.** How can a customer upload directly to our bucket if the bucket is private?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Our application gives the browser a presigned URL, a short-lived link for one recording. The browser uploads straight to the bucket, which stays private.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is: our application gives the browser a special link, called a presigned URL.

The browser sends the recording straight to the bucket with it.

It works like this. Our application signs the link with its own permissions.

The link is for one recording, and it has an expiry time.

The customer needs no AWS account and no password of their own.

S3 checks the expiry when the request arrives, then stores the recording.

The bucket stays private the whole time.

The thing to watch is that anyone who holds the link can use it.

They can use it many times until it expires, so we keep the expiry short.

In your case, we sign a fresh link for each upload.

How long does a customer need to upload a long call on a slow connection?

**Skeleton.** presigned URL, straight to bucket / signed with our permissions / anyone holding it, until expiry / a fresh link per upload

**Must say.**

- A presigned URL gives time-limited access to an object without changing the bucket policy, and it uses the credentials of the principal who generated it.
- A presigned URL lets someone upload a specific object to the bucket without AWS credentials or permissions of their own.
- The URL works only if its creator has permission for the operation, because a presigned URL is limited by the permissions of the user who created it.
- Anyone who holds the URL can use it, many times, until it expires, so the expiry should be short.

**Do not say.**

- "the link works only once". Say: A presigned URL can be used many times until its expiration date and time.
- "the customer needs an AWS account to upload". Say: A presigned URL lets someone upload a specific object without AWS credentials or permissions of their own.
- "the bucket has to be public for a moment". Say: The bucket stays private. A presigned URL gives time-limited access to an object without changing the bucket policy.

**Follow-up questions.**

- What is the longest expiry we can set on that link? A presigned URL created with the AWS CLI or an SDK can be valid for up to 7 days. If it is signed with temporary role credentials, it stops working when those credentials expire, whichever comes first.
- Our web page runs on another domain. Will the browser allow the upload? Only with a CORS configuration on the bucket. A browser normally blocks JavaScript requests to resources in a different domain. A CORS configuration on the bucket explicitly enables those cross-origin requests from your site.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

### Prompt 2

**A customer asks.** Should I put my old files in S3 Standard-IA or in Intelligent-Tiering?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Both cut the cost of rarely read data. Data read about once a month fits Standard-IA. If you do not know the pattern, choose Intelligent-Tiering.

**In 60 seconds.**

Both lower the storage cost of data that you rarely read.

The difference is who decides: you, or S3.

It works like this. Standard-IA is cheaper to store, but every read has a retrieval fee.

It also bills at least thirty days for each object.

Intelligent-Tiering watches each object and moves it to cheaper tiers when nobody reads it.

It has no retrieval fee, only a small monitoring charge per object.

The thing to watch is small objects.

Objects smaller than one hundred twenty-eight kilobytes stay in the Frequent Access tier.

And Standard-IA bills them as if they were one hundred twenty-eight kilobytes.

In your case, check two things: object size, and how often users open old data.

Do you know which old objects your users open again, and how big they are?

**Skeleton.** both cut cost of rare reads / Standard-IA: retrieval fee, minimum days / Intelligent-Tiering: moves objects, monitoring fee / small objects: check the size

**Must say.**

- S3 Intelligent-Tiering is the class for data with unknown, changing or unpredictable access patterns.
- Intelligent-Tiering has no retrieval charges, and it charges a small monthly monitoring and automation fee per object.
- S3 Standard-IA has a per-GB retrieval charge and a minimum storage duration of 30 days.
- Objects smaller than 128 KB are not auto-tiered in Intelligent-Tiering, and Standard-IA bills each of them as 128 KB.

**Do not say.**

- "Intelligent-Tiering has retrieval fees". Say: There are no retrieval charges in S3 Intelligent-Tiering. You pay a small monitoring and automation fee per object instead.
- "Standard-IA is always cheaper for old data". Say: Standard-IA adds a per-GB retrieval charge and bills at least 30 days and 128 KB per object, so small or short-lived objects can cost more there.

**Follow-up questions.**

- If an object in Intelligent-Tiering is read again, does it stay in the cheaper tier? No. When an object in the Infrequent Access or Archive Instant Access tier is accessed again, S3 moves it back to the Frequent Access tier automatically.
- Is there a minimum storage time in Intelligent-Tiering? No. S3 Intelligent-Tiering has no minimum storage duration. S3 Standard-IA and S3 One Zone-IA charge for at least 30 days.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

### Prompt 3

**A customer asks.** Object Lock governance mode or compliance mode: which one should we turn on for our records?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Both stop normal users from deleting a locked version. Compliance mode also stops administrators and the root user, and nobody can shorten it.

**In 60 seconds.**

Both modes lock a version of an object, so normal users can't delete it.

The difference is who can still remove the lock.

It works like this. In governance mode, a user with a special permission can bypass it.

That user also sends a bypass header with the request.

In compliance mode, no user can delete the version, not even the root user.

And nobody can shorten the retention period.

The thing to watch is that you can't turn Object Lock off later.

Versioning stays on for that bucket too.

So test your retention settings in governance mode before you use compliance mode.

In your case, the regulator decides.

Does your regulator require that nobody, not even an administrator, can delete a record early?

**Skeleton.** both lock a version / governance: bypass with permission / compliance: nobody, not even root / cannot turn it off later

**Must say.**

- In governance mode, users cannot delete a locked version unless they have special permission: s3:BypassGovernanceRetention plus the bypass header.
- In compliance mode, no user can overwrite or delete a protected version, including the root user, and its retention period cannot be shortened.
- After Object Lock is enabled on a bucket, you cannot disable Object Lock or Versioning for that bucket.
- AWS says to use compliance mode when no user, including the root user, should ever be able to delete objects during the retention period.

**Do not say.**

- "governance mode stops everyone". Say: In governance mode, a user with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention who sends the bypass header can delete a locked version or change its lock settings.
- "the root user can shorten a compliance retention period". Say: In compliance mode, no user can delete the version, including the root user, and its retention period cannot be shortened.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Is there any way to delete a compliance-mode record before its date? Only one: delete the AWS account that owns it. No user, including the root user, can delete or overwrite the version, and its retention period cannot be shortened. You can extend the retention period.
- What if a lawsuit needs a record kept after its retention date? Add a legal hold. It gives the same protection with no expiration date and stays until an authorized user removes it. It is independent of the retention period, so it keeps protecting the version after that period ends.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

### Prompt 4

**A customer asks.** S3 already has eleven nines of durability. Why should we pay for versioning or backups?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Durability means S3 won't lose your data. It doesn't protect you from your own deletes. Versioning keeps old versions, so you can restore them.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is: durability doesn't protect you from your own delete commands.

It works like this. Eleven nines means S3 is designed not to lose your data.

But when someone deletes an object, S3 deletes it right away.

AWS can't get it back for you.

With versioning on, a delete only adds a delete marker.

The old version stays, and you can restore it.

The thing to watch is cost: every old version is billed like a normal object.

So add a lifecycle rule that removes old versions after some days.

In your case, versioning is also what AWS Backup needs before it backs up a bucket.

If someone deleted a customer's recordings this morning, how would you get them back?

**Skeleton.** durability is not delete protection / a delete is immediate / versioning adds a delete marker / old versions cost: lifecycle rule

**Must say.**

- S3 is designed for 11 nines of durability, but durability does not protect against accidental or malicious deletes.
- When you tell S3 to delete data, it is deleted immediately and cannot be recovered by AWS.
- In a versioned bucket, a delete without a version ID adds a delete marker, and the earlier version is not permanently deleted.
- Normal S3 rates apply to every version of an object that is stored, so old versions keep costing money until they are deleted.

**Do not say.**

- "AWS can restore a deleted object for us". Say: When you tell S3 to delete data, it is deleted immediately and cannot be recovered by AWS. Versioning or a backup is how you get it back.
- "versioning stops all deletes". Say: A DELETE that names a version ID permanently deletes that version, and S3 adds no delete marker.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Can we stop someone from deleting old versions on purpose? Yes. For records that no user can delete before a date, use S3 Object Lock in compliance mode. MFA delete also asks for a second factor, but only the root user can turn it on, and you cannot use it with lifecycle rules, so it does not fit next to the rule I just suggested.
- Will versioning double our storage bill? It grows only when you overwrite or delete objects, because the old versions stay. Normal S3 rates apply to every stored version. A lifecycle rule can permanently delete noncurrent versions a set number of days after they become noncurrent.

</details>
